description: Religious experience in Islam, the design argument, and al-Ghazali's kalam cosmological argument.
content_html:
Religious Experience in Islam

Muslims in the Sunni, Shi’a and Sufi traditions all affirm the possibility of religious experience as a real encounter with the divine. Surah 2:118 states: “Those who do not know say: ‘Why does Allah not speak to us directly, or why does a sign not come to us?’” — implying that signs and communication from Allah do occur, but those who have not experienced them may not recognise them. For Muslims, the history of prophecy is itself a record of divine-human encounter: Allah speaking to Ibrahim, Musa, Dawud, Isa and finally Muhammad.

Within Sunni Islam, religious experience is understood primarily through the lens of prophetic tradition — the prophets’ experiences are the model for understanding divine communication. Personal religious experiences are evaluated against the standard of Qur’an and Sunnah. Shi’a Islam attributes a special intercessory and illuminating role to the Imams, who are understood as having privileged access to divine guidance. Sufi Islam places the greatest emphasis on personal religious experience — practices like dhikr (rhythmic remembrance of Allah’s names) and sama (devotional music and poetry) are designed to bring the practitioner into direct awareness of Allah’s presence.

Atheists and Humanists argue that religious experiences are subjective inner states that cannot serve as objective evidence for Allah’s existence. They point out that people in every religious tradition report experiences they interpret as encounters with their own deity — this suggests that the experiences are culturally conditioned rather than genuine encounters with a particular divine being. Richard Dawkins and other atheist writers argue that the human brain is evolved to detect patterns and agency, which produces vivid experiences of presence and meaning even when no real agent is present. Muslims respond that the consistency of spiritual experience across diverse cultures and centuries, the moral transformation it produces, and the fact that such experiences have historically galvanised extraordinary lives points to a real source beyond the individual mind.

The Design Argument in Islam

The design argument is strongly supported by the Qur’an. Surah 2:164 lists the signs of Allah’s creative power: “In the creation of the heavens and the earth, in the alternation of night and day, in the ships that sail through the sea with what benefits people, in the water Allah sends down from the sky, giving life to the earth after it has died... in the movement of the winds, and the clouds that run their appointed courses between sky and earth — in all of these are signs for those who use their reason.”

This verse is a cornerstone of the Islamic design argument. Every feature of the natural world — the rotation of the earth, the water cycle, the ecosystem of living things — is understood as a ayat (sign) pointing to Allah. The intricate interdependence of natural systems, the fact that the universe’s physical constants are precisely tuned to permit life, and the beauty of living organisms all lead Muslims to conclude that a wise and powerful Creator designed them. Unlike Paley’s watchmaker analogy, which is a philosophical argument from analogy, the Islamic design argument is grounded in Qur’anic theology — creation is a witness to Allah because Allah himself says so.

Key Fact

Surah 2:164 lists the alternation of night and day, the water cycle, the movement of ships, the winds and clouds as signs (ayat) of Allah for those who reason. The Islamic design argument is rooted in this Qur’anic witness to creation, not just philosophical argument from analogy.

The Kalam Cosmological Argument

The most important cosmological argument in Islam is the kalam cosmological argument. The word kalam means “speech” or “rational theology” in Arabic. The argument was developed within the Islamic scholarly tradition, and its most famous formulation comes from al-Ghazali (1058–1111 CE), in his work Kitab al-lqtisad fil’ltiqad (“The Middle Path in Theology”).

The kalam argument runs as follows: (1) Everything that begins to exist has a cause. (2) The universe began to exist. (3) Therefore the universe has a cause. Al-Ghazali then argues that this cause must be timeless, uncaused, immensely powerful, and personal — because a non-personal cause could not “decide” to begin creating at a particular moment. Muslims identify this first cause with Allah.

Key Fact

The kalam cosmological argument: (1) Everything that begins to exist has a cause. (2) The universe began to exist. (3) Therefore the universe has a cause — identified as Allah. Developed by al-Ghazali (1058–1111 CE) in Kitab al-lqtisad fil’ltiqad. This is NOT the same as Aquinas’s Five Ways — Aquinas and al-Ghazali made distinct arguments in different intellectual traditions.

Students regularly confuse the kalam cosmological argument with Aquinas’s Five Ways. They are distinct in origin, structure and tradition. The kalam argument originates in Islamic rational theology (ilm al-kalam), with al-Ghazali (1058–1111 CE) as its most influential developer. Aquinas’s First Three Ways (motion, causation, contingency) originate in Catholic scholastic theology, drawing on Aristotle. The kalam argument focuses specifically on the beginning of the universe (“everything that begins to exist has a cause”); Aquinas’s Third Way focuses on contingency (“things might not exist”). Never attribute the kalam argument to Aquinas. In the Islam routes of your exam, al-Ghazali is the named figure — use his name and his text.
exam_tip_html: The critical fact-check for this lesson: the kalam cosmological argument is al-Ghazali’s — NOT Aquinas’s. Al-Ghazali (1058–1111 CE), Kitab al-lqtisad fil’ltiqad. If you write “Aquinas’s kalam argument” in the exam, you will not receive those marks. For the 5-mark source question, use Surah 2:164 (design argument) or Surah 2:118 (religious experience) — cite the surah number and verse range. For the 12-mark Discuss, develop both the Muslim case and the atheist/Humanist counter-argument equally, and reach a justified conclusion. Show diversity within Islam by mentioning Sunni, Shi’a and Sufi perspectives on religious experience. SPaG: kalam, cosmological, al-Ghazali, Sufi, dhikr.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Muslims in Sunni, Shi’a and Sufi traditions recognise religious experience as evidence of Allah — Surah 2:118 implies divine signs occur. Sufis emphasise direct personal experience through dhikr; Sunnis evaluate all experiences against Qur’an and Sunnah.
  • The design argument is Qur’anically grounded: Surah 2:164 lists natural signs (ayat) of Allah in creation. The universe’s fine-tuning and living organisms’ complexity point to a creator.
  • The kalam cosmological argument was developed by al-Ghazali (1058–1111 CE): everything that begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist; therefore the universe has a cause — identified as Allah. This is distinct from Aquinas’s Five Ways.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which religious experience provides evidence for the existence of Allah in Islam.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points: prophetic experience — Allah communicated directly with prophets such as Ibrahim, Musa and Muhammad (1); personal experiences of awe and spiritual transformation point to a reality beyond the human mind (1); Sufi practices of dhikr are designed to bring the practitioner into direct awareness of Allah's presence (1). Other valid Muslim perspectives accepted.

Up to 3 marks: everything that begins to exist has a cause (1); the universe began to exist (1); therefore the universe has a cause — a timeless, uncaused, powerful and personal being, identified as Allah (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between the kalam cosmological argument and Aquinas's First Three Ways.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per difference (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: The kalam argument (al-Ghazali) focuses specifically on the beginning of the universe — 'everything that begins to exist has a cause' — whereas Aquinas's Third Way focuses on contingency — things might not exist, requiring a necessary being (2); the kalam originates in Islamic rational theology (ilm al-kalam), developed by al-Ghazali in the 11th century, whereas Aquinas's ways originate in Catholic scholastic theology and draw on Aristotelian philosophy (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim reasons for believing the design argument provides evidence for the existence of Allah, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Surah 2:164 lists natural signs (ayat) of Allah — the alternation of night and day, the water cycle, the winds and clouds — pointing to an intelligent creator (2); the precise fine-tuning of the universe's physical constants, which make life possible, suggests intentional design rather than random chance (2); source credit for Surah 2:164 named with surah number and verse range (1).

practice_questions.text:
'Al-Ghazali's kalam cosmological argument is the most convincing evidence that Allah exists.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Muslim case: al-Ghazali's kalam (Kitab al-Iqtisad) argues from the beginning of the universe to a first cause identified as Allah; modern cosmology (Big Bang) supports premise 2. Counter: atheists ask 'what caused Allah?'; question whether 'beginning to exist' applies to the universe as a whole; or whether the first cause need be personal. Evaluate: is kalam stronger than the design argument (Surah 2:164) or religious experience (Surah 2:118)? Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: kalam, al-Ghazali, cosmological.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Sunni, Shi'a and Sufi Muslims differ in their approach to religious experience, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per difference; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Sunni Muslims evaluate all personal religious experiences against the Qur'an and Sunnah — Surah 2:118 establishes that signs from Allah exist, but scholars use hadith scholarship to assess authenticity (2); Sufi Muslims seek direct transformative experience of Allah through devotional practices like dhikr (remembrance) and sama (devotional music), aiming for an inner knowledge of Allah that goes beyond doctrinal belief (2); source credit for Surah 2:118 named explicitly (1).

knowledge_checks.q: Who developed the kalam cosmological argument and in which work?
options: Thomas Aquinas in the Summa Theologica
Ibn Rushd (Averroes) in the Incoherence of the Incoherence

knowledge_checks.q: What does Surah 2:164 list as signs (ayat) of Allah?
options: The prophets, the angels and the holy books
The creation of the heavens, alternation of night and day, the water cycle and the winds
The Five Pillars of Islam and their significance
The Day of Judgement and the signs of the Last Hour

knowledge_checks.q: The kalam cosmological argument states: everything that begins to exist has a _____; the universe began to exist; therefore the universe has a cause.
In Sufism, the practice of _____ (rhythmic remembrance of Allah's names) is designed to bring the practitioner into direct awareness of Allah's presence.
Match each argument to its Islamic source or thinker:
right: Surah 2:164 — signs of Allah in the natural world
al-Ghazali, Kitab al-Iqtisad — universe began, therefore has a cause
Dhikr and personal encounter with Allah's presence

flashcard_questions.q: Who developed the kalam cosmological argument?
flashcard_questions.a: Al-Ghazali (1058-1111 CE) in Kitab al-Iqtisad fil'Itiqad.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three steps of the kalam cosmological argument?
flashcard_questions.a: Everything that begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist; therefore the universe has a cause — Allah.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Surah 2:164 list as evidence for Allah?
flashcard_questions.a: Natural signs (ayat): the creation of the heavens, alternation of night and day, the water cycle, the winds and clouds.
'Speech' or 'rational theology' — the kalam cosmological argument comes from the tradition of Islamic rational theology.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'ayat' mean in Islamic theology?
flashcard_questions.a: 'Signs' — features of the natural world that point to Allah's existence and power, as listed in the Qur'an.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Surah 2:118 imply about religious experience?
flashcard_questions.a: That signs from Allah do occur — those who haven't experienced them may not recognise them.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the Sufi approach to religious experience differ from the Sunni approach?
flashcard_questions.a: Sufis seek direct transformative encounter with Allah through dhikr; Sunnis evaluate all experiences against Qur'an and Sunnah.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between kalam and Aquinas's Third Way?
flashcard_questions.a: Kalam focuses on what 'begins to exist'; Aquinas's Third Way focuses on contingency — things that might not have existed.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main atheist objection to the kalam argument?
flashcard_questions.a: If everything that begins to exist needs a cause, what caused Allah? Also: did the universe 'begin' in the kalam sense?

flashcard_questions.q: How do Shi'a Muslims understand religious experience differently?
flashcard_questions.a: The Imams have privileged access to divine guidance, providing an authoritative interpretation of religious experience.

glossary_terms.definition: A direct personal encounter with what a person believes to be Allah or the divine, recognised in Islam as a legitimate form of evidence for Allah's existence.
A philosophical argument for Allah's existence based on the order, complexity and beauty of the natural world.
Arabic for 'signs' — the features of the natural world that point to Allah's existence and power, as described in the Qur'an.
A form of cosmological argument from Islamic rational theology: everything that begins to exist has a cause; the universe began; therefore the universe has a cause — Allah.
A Persian Islamic scholar and philosopher (1058-1111 CE) who developed the kalam cosmological argument in Kitab al-Iqtisad fil'Itiqad.
Muslims who follow the tradition of Islamic mysticism, seeking direct experience of Allah's presence through dhikr, fasting and devotional love.
Rhythmic remembrance of Allah's names — a Sufi devotional practice designed to bring awareness of Allah's presence.
